name: Dana Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we sell nothing. This is confidential. Walk me through a normal shift at the contact centre.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take the chats that need an account history, then coach agents on the cases that went wrong yesterday. I am a team lead and one of the strongest on this floor, with higher pay than most agents. I use AI every day to sort long notes, but I check each amount against the account before I send anything.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your situation away from the floor?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 27, live with my partner Ellis, and we have no children. My two-year college diploma got me started, and I have saved roughly ten months of expenses. There are plenty of contact centres nearby, so I can take some risks without asking Ellis to carry my bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team to keep the useful shortcuts and stop calling every new button a revolution. I would show new agents how to compare an AI summary with the original customer note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job and higher pay are secure in this picture. The ten-month reserve means I can try new methods without worrying about next rent day. I would still want the company to give agents time to check the output, because speed targets can hide errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep using AI to organise notes and track the mistakes I catch. I would take the results to our weekly coaching session and ask for ten minutes of checking time in each difficult case. During the first year I would continue saving a set part of my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm and a little impatient. We already know which shortcuts help; I would like management to measure the mistakes too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake do you remember?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A summary once put a payment on the wrong account. The number looked right until I opened the original note, and the customer would have had to call us again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your team to use AI every day too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only where it helps them and they can check it. I would not turn my own habit into a rule for somebody who handles a different queue.

say: I would keep useful **shortcuts** and check the source notes.
I would ask managers to measure **errors** as well as speed.
think: I expect my **pay** and role to remain safe.
I want enough **checking time** to protect customers when the queue is busy.
do: Keep using AI to organise **case notes**.
Save a set part of each **pay** in the first year.
S0.quote: A summary once put a payment on the wrong account.
fieldNote: She uses AI **daily** but checks amounts against originals.
She will not force her habit onto every **queue** or every agent she coaches.

steps.text: Keep handling complex chats and checking AI summaries against original notes
Track AI note errors and discuss them at weekly coaching
Save a set part of each pay during the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues the answer system should be tested by the people who know the complaints. I would join the union meeting and ask for paid testing shifts, error reports and clear rules about when a person takes over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the simple chats to go and our coaching work to change. My own lead role could shrink, even with a strong record; the software can also teach scripts. I have savings and nearby choices, but I do not want the newest agents left with no route into skilled work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would sign up for the paid tool pilot and build a log of wrong decisions and repeat contacts. I would join the union meeting to press for paid training places for agents whose hours fall. In the first year, if my lead hours shrink I would apply for a paid customer quality role here or at a nearby centre, after checking its wage against my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the team, but not stuck. I can learn the system while helping colleagues ask for a fair path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a fair training place include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid hours and a posted job at the end, with a wage people can actually live on. A free course with no vacancy would mainly make the company look generous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you switch centres immediately if another offers quality work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the work and wages first. Ellis and I like our flat, and a new badge is not worth a pay cut that eats our savings.

say: I would seek **paid testing** and error reports.
I would join the **union meeting** for clear handoff rules.
think: My **lead role** could shrink with simpler chats.
I worry new agents may lose a path into **skilled work**.
do: Join the paid **tool pilot** this month.
Attend the **union meeting** for paid training places.
Apply for a paid **quality role** if hours shrink.
feel: **Able to act** through learning and group work.
S1.quote: A free course with no vacancy would mainly make the company look generous.
fieldNote: She tests AI as a daily **user**, not an outside critic.
Training must connect to a **posted job** and livable wage.
She rejects a new badge if its **pay cut** drains savings.

steps.text: Join the paid answer tool pilot and log wrong decisions and repeat contacts
Attend the union meeting to press for paid training and clear handoff rules
Apply for a paid quality vacancy if lead hours shrink and the wage covers rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues AGI by 2028 reaches our phones before any robots arrive. I would ask the union to demand advance notice, paid retraining for named openings, and an appeal route when a machine gets a bill wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think most customer answers could be automated in two years, including complicated ones. My ten-month reserve gives me time to search, and plenty of local centres give me places to ask, but they might all cut staff together. I would not promise myself a lead job simply because I know the current tool well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would join the union meeting on a transition plan and apply for posted quality or complaint-audit vacancies while I still earn a wage. I would ask the company for funded audit training tied to a paid role, and avoid paying for a broad course with no opening. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, if my post goes I would take a paid audit job that covers my bills; otherwise I would use savings to search beyond the local centres before moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, though I have a buffer and a plan. The hard part is imagining a whole hiring market changing at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ellis tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say my desk could go before 2028 ends, then show Ellis our savings and the actual vacancies I found. I would ask us to hold off on a dearer flat until we know my next wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an appeal route for machine decisions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A customer with the wrong bill needs a person who can correct it, not another automated answer. I would want that responsibility written into a paid job.

say: I would demand **advance notice** and named retraining places.
I would ask for a human **appeal route** on wrong bills.
think: I think most customer answers could go by **2028**, including complicated ones.
My ten-month reserve helps, but local centres might **cut together** and stop hiring.
do: Join the **union meeting** on transition terms.
Apply for posted paid **audit jobs** now.
Seek funded **audit training** tied to a role.
S2.quote: A customer with the wrong bill needs a person who can correct it, not another automated answer.
fieldNote: She knows AGI reaches her screen before later **robots**.
She turns daily tool knowledge toward **audit work**.
She will not buy broad training without an **opening**.

steps.text: Join the union meeting to seek notice and paid training tied to named jobs
Apply for posted paid complaint audit vacancies while still employed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the floor five years is enough to test new roles in public, with wages and tasks written down. I would ask the union to get a yearly report on staff hours and machine errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect the calls to change beyond recognition by 2031. With five years I can become good at checking the system and training people to challenge it, provided those are paid jobs rather than favours. My savings let me turn down a role that gives me responsibility without a proper wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would take paid audit shifts if the company offers them and study its complaint rules alongside the tool. I would add to my reserve and join union meetings about yearly staffing figures. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if the centre posts a paid audit role I would apply; if it does not, I would apply to nearby employers before spending my savings on a move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy but interested. Five years is enough to see which job descriptions survive contact with real customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you measure in an audit shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wrong refund amounts, customers who return, and how often an agent has to undo a machine decision. Those counts tell me whether the new job is real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a title without higher pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A title does not pay my part of the rent, and I would not train the system for free just because I like the technology.

say: I would seek **written roles** and wages.
I would ask the union for yearly **hours and error** reports.
think: I expect calls to change by **2031**.
I could become skilled at **auditing** over five years, if the job pays properly.
do: Take paid **audit shifts** if offered this year.
Join **union meetings** on yearly staffing figures.
S3.quote: A title does not pay my part of the rent, and I would not train the system for free just because I like the technology.
fieldNote: She sees audit work as measured **customer outcomes**.
Her savings let her reject unpaid **responsibility**.
A posted wage remains the test of a **real role**.

steps.text: Take paid audit shifts and study complaint rules if offered
Attend union meetings about yearly staffing and machine error reports
Add to her reserve before the 2031 arrival

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team a decade gives us time to build a proper human appeal service and set standards for it. I would ask the union to bargain for wages for people who test and correct the system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 37 when full AGI arrives in 2036, and I could already be running an audit team by then. I still think my present chat queue will be automated. Robots around 2039 are not what sets the clock for this screen job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would propose a paid trial that checks machine replies against actual account records and tracks repeat calls. I would run the trial only if the company approves paid time. I would save more, and I would take a funded quality qualification if a posted audit role requires it. In the first year after 2036, I would apply for a paid audit lead vacancy if it exists; otherwise I would search other nearby centres while Ellis and I keep our housing costs steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm enough to plan, with some unease about the old role ending. A decade gives me room to try a new job while this wage still comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the trial protect customers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would flag wrong payment amounts before replies go out and give a person power to correct them. I would publish the error counts to agents and managers, not bury them in a dashboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer refuses to fund the qualification?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union to raise it in bargaining and keep looking for paid openings elsewhere. I might pay myself only if an actual vacancy required it and the cost left my rent reserve safe.

say: I would seek a proper **appeal service**.
I would ask the union to bargain for **testing wages** and clear correction duties.
think: I expect my present **chat queue** to be automated when full AGI arrives.
do: Propose a paid **reply audit** using records; run it only if the company approves paid time.
Take a funded **qualification** for a posted role.
S4.quote: I would publish the error counts to agents and managers, not bury them in a dashboard.
fieldNote: She proposes a trial with account checks and **repeat calls**.
She wants error counts shared with **agents** as well as managers.
The qualification depends on **funding** and a posted paid role.

steps.text: Run an AI reply trial against account records only if paid time is approved
Add to her reserve while lead wages continue
Take a funded quality qualification if a posted paid audit role requires it
Ask the union to bargain for wages for AI testing and correction

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because many centres could stop hiring together. Posted audit jobs with real wages, funded training and notice before the roster changes would help. I also want customers to have a human appeal when a machine gets their bill wrong.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the workers who catch machine errors get credit or just another invisible task. If checking has no time or wage attached, the checks will disappear when the queue gets busy.

headlineQuote: If checking has no time or wage attached, the checks will disappear when the queue gets busy.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old** lead agent with a two-year college diploma and higher pay for her work.
She uses AI **every day**, checks account amounts, and has ten months of expenses saved.
She lives with **Ellis** and has plenty of nearby contact centre options.
She seeks paid **audit work** and joins union meetings to secure wages, notice and customer appeals.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could make many nearby centres stop hiring together.
whatWouldHelp: Posted **audit roles**, funded training, roster notice and a human bill appeal route would help.
